english: Hello, this is ○○○ from the ○○ team
usage: Hello, this is Kim Minsu from the Marketing team
The standard opening line of almost every work email
Hello, this is ○○○, the person in charge of ○○
When the reader may not know you; states your role
This is Assistant Manager ○○○ from ○○ Company
To an external party; lead with company + title
Good day, this is ○○○ from the ○○ team
More formal 하십니까 for very senior or official mail
examples: 안녕하세요, 영업팀 김민수입니다.
Hello, this is Kim Minsu from the Sales team.
Minimum viable opening: greeting + team + name + 입니다
안녕하세요, 영업팀 김민수입니다. 어제 통화드린 건으로 메일 드립니다.
Hello, this is Kim Minsu from Sales. I'm writing about the matter we discussed by phone yesterday.
Greeting then immediately state WHY you're writing — the professional pattern
A: 안녕하세요, ABC회사 영업팀 김민수 대리입니다. 견적 관련해서 연락드렸습니다. / B: 네, 안녕하세요. 말씀하세요.
A: Hello, this is Assistant Manager Kim Minsu from ABC Company's Sales team. I'm contacting you about a quote. / B: Yes, hello. Please go ahead.
External first-contact exchange: company + team + name + title + reason; the reader's 말씀하세요 confirms the opening worked
nuance: Korean work emails almost always open with 안녕하세요 + your identity in the pattern [team/company] + [name] + [optional title] + 입니다. Skipping this feels abrupt and rude in Korean office culture, where establishing who you are before the request is a non-negotiable social script. The verb 입니다 means 'I am ~', and you state your own name plainly — never with honorific 님 attached to yourself (김민수님입니다 is wrong; 님 honors others). Title order differs from English: Korean says 김민수 대리 (name THEN rank), not 대리 김민수. The more formal variant 안녕하십니까 (합쇼체) is used for very senior recipients, official announcements, or letters; everyday inter-office mail uses 안녕하세요. The classic English-speaker trap is translating 'My name is' as 제 이름은 ~예요, which sounds like a textbook drill rather than a professional self-introduction; the natural business form is simply [name]입니다. Also avoid opening with 저는 ~ every time — Korean drops the 'I' once context is clear, so 김민수입니다 alone is cleaner.

structuredNuance.t: Korean work emails open with 안녕하세요 + [team/company] + [name] + [optional title] + 입니다. This is non-negotiable: jumping straight to the request feels abrupt and rude in Korean office culture, where establishing identity first is a social script. 입니다 means 'I am ~' — you state your own name plainly without attaching 님 to yourself.

안녕하세요 + 입니다 is the everyday polite (합쇼체) level safe for all internal and external email. Upgrade to 안녕하십니까 (one notch more formal) for very senior recipients, official letters, or company-wide announcements. Never use 안녕 (반말) in any professional email regardless of how well you know the colleague.
chips: 안녕 — 반말, never in work email

structuredNuance.t: 안녕하십니까 vs. 안녕하세요: both are 존댓말 but 하십니까 is one notch more formal/official (합쇼체), expected in announcements, to C-suite, or in print. For a normal intra-team or client email, 하세요 is the default. Switching to 하십니까 unnecessarily can feel stiff or bureaucratic.

Minimal: 안녕하세요, 김민수입니다. / With team: 안녕하세요, 마케팅팀 김민수입니다. / With title: 안녕하세요, 마케팅팀 김민수 대리입니다. / External full: 안녕하세요, ABC회사 마케팅팀 김민수 대리입니다. Add layers based on how well the reader knows you — more layers for strangers or external contacts.

Do not write 제 이름은 김민수예요 — that is a textbook casual self-intro, not business email. Do not attach 님 to your own name (김민수님입니다 is self-elevating and wrong). Do not put title before name (대리 김민수 is the English order; Korean is 김민수 대리). And do not add 저는 every sentence — Korean omits the subject once established.

mistakes: Writing 제 이름은 김민수예요 in a work email.
That's a casual/textbook self-intro. Professional email states identity as 김민수입니다 (or 팀 + 이름 + 입니다), not '내 이름은 ~예요'.
Attaching 님 to your own name: 김민수님입니다.
님 is an honorific for OTHERS. Referring to yourself you drop it: 김민수입니다. Using 님 on yourself sounds self-elevating and wrong.
Ordering title before name: 대리 김민수입니다.
Korean puts rank AFTER the name: 김민수 대리입니다. The English order 'Assistant Manager Kim' reversed sounds off.

english: Please take note / for your reference
usage: Polite-formal; asks the reader to keep it in mind
Just for your reference (no action needed)
Signals it's FYI only, nothing to do
Curt note-style ending, internal memos/superiors to juniors
examples: 아래 내용 참고 부탁드립니다.
Please take note of the content below.
Points the reader to information you have included — no action expected
지난번과 일정이 변경되었으니 참고 부탁드립니다.
The schedule has changed from last time, so please take note.
Used to flag a change the reader should simply be aware of
A: 이 데이터는 최신 기준입니다. 참고 부탁드립니다. / B: 네, 확인했습니다. 감사합니다.
A: This data is based on the latest figures. Please take note. / B: Understood, I've seen it. Thank you.
Short A/B exchange showing 참고 as a pure FYI hand-off with a polite acknowledgment reply
nuance: 참고 부탁드립니다 is 참고 ('reference/consultation', Sino-Korean 參考) + 부탁드립니다 ('I humbly request'), meaning 'please keep this in mind / for your reference'. It is a soft, information-sharing closer: you are not demanding action, just asking the reader to be AWARE of something. The crucial contrast with 참조 (參照): in email, 참조 is the CC field (참조: 박과장님) — it names who is copied — whereas 참고 means 'for your information'. English speakers confuse these because both translate loosely as 'reference'; writing 참조 부탁드립니다 to mean 'please note this' reads as 'please CC this'. A second contrast: 참고하세요 (plain imperative) is fine to juniors or peers but can sound directive to a superior; 참고 부탁드립니다 with humble 부탁드리다 is safer upward. 참고 is a 하다-noun, so to make it a verb you need 참고하다 — never 참고 주세요 (you cannot 'give' a reference). The softer 참고하시기 바랍니다 or 참고만 해 주세요 (FYI-only, no action) are useful variants.

structuredNuance.t: 참고 부탁드립니다 means 'please keep this in mind / for your reference'. It is a soft information-sharing closer — you are not demanding an action, just asking the reader to be AWARE. The humble 부탁드리다 frame keeps the register appropriate for any level of seniority.

Safe to send upward (to bosses, clients) because 부탁드리다 is humble. Downward or to peers you can use the plainer 참고하세요 or the note-style 참고 바람. In announcements or notices, 참고하시기 바랍니다 is the more official written form.

참고 부탁드립니다 (FYI, no action needed) vs. 확인 부탁드립니다 (please check/confirm something) vs. 검토 부탁드립니다 (please examine and judge critically). The three form a spectrum from lightest (참고) to heaviest ask (검토). Also: 참조 (參照) = the CC field — writing 참조 부탁드립니다 to mean 'please note' is wrong.

참고 부탁드립니다 → 참고하시기 바랍니다 (more formal/official) → 참고만 해 주세요 (FYI-only, explicitly no action) → 참고 바람 (curt memo note, downward only). To soften further: 참고로 알려 드립니다 ('I'm letting you know for reference').

Do not confuse 참고 (參考, FYI) with 참조 (參照, the CC field). Do not say 참고 주세요 — 참고 is a 하다-noun; you cannot 'give' it. The verb is 참고하다, so the request form is 참고해 주세요 or 참고 부탁드립니다. Also avoid 체크 — Konglish; use 참고 for FYI and 확인 for confirmation.

mistakes: Confusing 참고 with 참조.
참조 is the email CC line ('참조: ~님'); 참고 means 'for your reference'. Writing 참조 부탁드립니다 to mean 'please note' sounds like 'please CC'. Use 참고 for FYI.
Saying 참고 주세요.
참고 is a 하다-noun; you can't 'give' it. The verb is 참고하다, so it's 참고해 주세요 or 참고 부탁드립니다, never 참고 주세요.
Using bare 참고하세요 to a senior.
The plain imperative can feel directive upward. To a superior, soften to 참고 부탁드립니다 or 참고하시기 바랍니다.

usage: Polite-formal; states the file is attached
Adds 드리다 to sound a touch more courteous
Pairs the attachment with a request to open it
Crisp present-tense form, common in quick mail
examples: 요청하신 자료 첨부했습니다.
I've attached the materials you requested.
Links the attachment directly to what they asked for
견적서 첨부해 드리니 확인 부탁드립니다.
I'm attaching the quote, so please review it.
첨부 + follow-up 확인 부탁드립니다 — the most common two-line pattern
A: 수정된 보고서 다시 보내 주실 수 있나요? / B: 네, 수정본 첨부드립니다. 이전 파일은 삭제해 주세요.
A: Could you resend the revised report? / B: Yes, I'm attaching the revised version. Please delete the previous file.
Real A/B exchange: resending a corrected file with a deletion request
nuance: 첨부했습니다 is 첨부 ('attachment', Sino-Korean 添附) + 하다 in formal past: 'I have attached'. It is the standard line for 'please find attached'. The everyday options are 첨부했습니다 (I attached), 첨부합니다 (I'm attaching), and the warmer 첨부해 드립니다 / 첨부드립니다, where 드리다 ('to do for someone, humbly') signals you are doing the reader a service — common and polite upward. The key contrast: 첨부 (添附) is electronically attaching a FILE to an email, while 동봉 (同封) is physically enclosing something in a paper envelope — do not write 동봉했습니다 for an emailed PDF. A frequent English-speaker pitfall is the over-literal 'please find attached' rendered as 첨부된 것을 찾아 주세요 ('please go look for the attached thing'), which sounds like the file is missing; simply state 첨부했습니다. Watch the particle: it is 파일을 첨부했습니다 (object 을/를), not 파일에 첨부. And 첨부 is a 하다-noun: to ask THEM to attach something, use the verb: 첨부해 주세요, never 첨부 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 첨부했습니다 means 'I have attached' — the standard line for 'please find attached'. The everyday options are 첨부했습니다 (past), 첨부합니다 (present), and the warmer 첨부해 드립니다 / 첨부드립니다, where 드리다 signals you are doing the reader a service. All three are correct; choice depends on how much courtesy you want to show.

Use 첨부했습니다 or 첨부합니다 in standard business email to any level. Upgrade to 첨부해 드립니다 or 첨부드립니다 for clients or senior recipients. 첨부 파일 확인 부탁드립니다 is often added as a follow-up line to nudge the reader to actually open it.

첨부 (添附, electronic attachment) vs. 동봉 (同封, physically enclosed in a paper envelope). Do not use 동봉했습니다 in an email — it signals a letter with enclosures. Also: 첨부하다 (to attach) vs. 파일을 보내다 (to send a file, more casual).
첨부했습니다 → 첨부해 드립니다 (more courteous) → 첨부드립니다 (compact humble form) → 파일 첨부합니다 (quick present-tense). To ask the reader to check: 첨부 파일 확인 부탁드립니다. To resend: 다시 첨부드립니다 / 재첨부드립니다.

Do not write 첨부된 것을 찾아 주세요 ('please go look for the attached thing') — it sounds like the file is lost. Do not use 동봉했습니다 for an email PDF. Watch the particle: 파일'을' 첨부했습니다 (object marker), not 파일'에' 첨부. And never say 첨부 주세요 — 첨부 is a 하다-noun; to request attachment use 첨부해 주세요.

mistakes: Translating 'please find attached' as 첨부된 것을 찾아 주세요.
찾다 ('to look for') makes it sound like the file is missing. Just state 첨부했습니다 or 첨부 파일 확인 부탁드립니다.
Using 동봉 for an email file.
동봉 (同封) is enclosing something in a physical envelope. For an emailed file use 첨부 (添附): 파일을 첨부했습니다.
Saying 첨부 주세요 when asking someone to attach.
첨부 is a 하다-noun; it can't be 'given'. Use the verb: 첨부해 주세요 ('please attach it').

usage: The default polite-formal request to review something
Softer, slightly less stiff than 드립니다
Adds an explicit reply step after checking
examples: 아래 금액에 이상 없는지 확인 부탁드립니다.
Please confirm the amounts below are correct.
Verify a specific figure — the most common use
일정 가능하신지 확인 부탁드립니다.
Please confirm whether the schedule works for you.
확인 used to confirm availability, not just read content
A: 내일 오전 10시에 회의실 예약했습니다. 확인 부탁드립니다. / B: 확인했습니다. 참석하겠습니다.
A: I've booked the meeting room for 10 a.m. tomorrow. Please confirm. / B: Confirmed. I'll attend.
A/B exchange: confirmation request and acknowledgment — the most natural email pair
nuance: 확인 부탁드립니다 is 확인 ('confirmation/checking', Sino-Korean 確認) + 부탁드립니다 ('I humbly ask'), the single most common closing request in Korean work email. 확인 covers both 'verify it is correct' and 'acknowledge you have seen it', so it is wonderfully versatile. The politeness lives in 부탁드리다 (humble 'to request'), making this safe upward to bosses and clients. The near-synonym contrast: 검토 (檢討) means a deeper REVIEW — reading critically, forming a judgment — while 확인 is a lighter 'check/confirm'. Asking a senior to 확인 a number is fine; if you want their considered opinion, use 검토 부탁드립니다. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the loanword 체크 (체크 부탁드립니다) — understandable but casual Konglish; professional mail uses 확인. Another trap is the plain imperative 확인하세요, which can sound curt or bossy upward; 확인 부탁드립니다 frames the same request as a humble ask. 확인 is a 하다-noun; if you want the full verb form, it is 확인해 주세요, never 확인 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 확인 부탁드립니다 is the single most common closing request in Korean work email — 'please check/confirm this'. 확인 covers both 'verify it is correct' and 'acknowledge you have seen it'. The humble 부탁드리다 makes it safe to send upward to any boss or client.

Safe at all levels because of 부탁드리다. Downward, you can use the slightly brisker 확인해 주세요. For official notices or formal documents, 확인해 주시기 바랍니다 is the most elevated written form. Never use the bare 확인하세요 upward — it sounds like an order.

확인 (light check/confirm) vs. 검토 (深 review with judgment) vs. 참고 (FYI, no action). Choosing wrong signals a mismatch: 확인 for a strategy doc undersells what you need; 검토 for just looking at a number is overstated.
확인 부탁드립니다 → 확인 부탁드려요 (softer) → 확인해 주시기 바랍니다 (official) → 확인 후 회신 부탁드립니다 (check then reply) → 확인 후 연락 주시면 감사하겠습니다 (most courteous conditional).

Do not write 체크 부탁드립니다 — 체크 is casual Konglish. Do not send bare 확인하세요 to a boss — it sounds like an order. Do not write 확인 주세요 — 확인 is a 하다-noun; the correct verb form is 확인해 주세요. And do not use 확인 when you actually need considered feedback — use 검토 instead.

mistakes: Writing 체크 부탁드립니다.
체크 is casual Konglish. Professional Korean email uses 확인: 확인 부탁드립니다.
Sending bare 확인하세요 to a boss or client.
The plain imperative can sound like an order. Soften with the humble request frame: 확인 부탁드립니다 or 확인해 주시기 바랍니다.
Using 확인 when you need a considered review.
확인 is a light 'check/confirm'. If you want them to critically examine and give feedback, ask 검토 부탁드립니다 instead.

usage: Polite-formal; asks for a written response
답장 is the everyday word for a reply/letter back
I'd be grateful for your reply
Attaches a deadline to the reply request
examples: 검토 후 회신 부탁드립니다.
Please reply after reviewing.
Asks them to review first, then respond — the standard two-step
바쁘시겠지만 금요일까지 회신 부탁드립니다.
I know you're busy, but please reply by Friday.
바쁘시겠지만 softens a deadline request so it does not feel pushy
A: 참석 가능하신지 회신 주시면 일정 잡겠습니다. / B: 네, 참석 가능합니다. 잘 부탁드립니다.
A: If you could reply whether you can attend, I'll set the schedule. / B: Yes, I can attend. Looking forward to it.
A/B: reply request tied to a next action, and the recipient's polite confirmation
nuance: 회신 부탁드립니다 is 회신 ('reply/response', Sino-Korean 回信) + 부탁드립니다, asking the reader to write back — the formal email staple for 'please respond'. 회신 is the crisp, businesslike word slightly more formal than the everyday 답장 ('a letter/message back'); both are correct, but 회신 dominates in professional mail and 답장 feels a touch more personal or casual. The contrast to watch: 회신 (the act of replying, general) vs. 답변 (答辯, the ANSWER itself to a specific question). If you posed a concrete question and want that answer, 답변 부탁드립니다 fits; for a general 'please get back to me', use 회신. The English-speaker pitfall is over-literal 'reply to me' as 저에게 회신해 주세요 — 저에게 ('to me') is redundant and heavy; 회신 부탁드립니다 already implies the direction. Another trap is treating 'respond' as 반응 (反應, a physical or emotional reaction) — 반응 부탁드립니다 sounds like asking for a like or reaction, not an email reply.

structuredNuance.t: 회신 부탁드립니다 asks the reader to write back — the formal email staple for 'please respond'. 회신 is the crisp, businesslike word for a reply, slightly more formal than everyday 답장. The humble 부탁드리다 makes it safe upward and to clients.

회신 부탁드립니다 is the standard upward/outward form. For extra courtesy — especially to clients or senior executives — upgrade to 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다. With a deadline, add the date: ○일까지 회신 부탁드립니다. Soften deadline requests with 바쁘시겠지만 so they do not read as demands.

회신 (a reply, getting back to you, general) vs. 답변 (答辯, the answer to a specific question you asked). Pose a direct question → 답변 부탁드립니다. Want them to just get back to you → 회신 부탁드립니다. Using 답변 where 회신 fits is not wrong but overly formal.
회신 부탁드립니다 → 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다 (conditional, gentler) → ○일까지 회신 부탁드립니다 (deadline) → 검토 후 회신 부탁드립니다 (review then reply). The everyday synonym 답장 부탁드립니다 is fine in internal or less formal mail.

Do not add 저에게 ('to me') — 회신 부탁드립니다 already implies the direction; the extra pronoun sounds heavy. Do not use 반응 부탁드립니다 — 반응 (反應) is a physical or emotional reaction, not an email reply. Do not translate 'please get back to me' as 저한테 돌아와 주세요 — 돌아오다 is physical return.

mistakes: Saying 반응 부탁드립니다 for 'please respond'.
반응 is a reaction/response in a physical sense. For an email reply use 회신 부탁드립니다 or 답장 부탁드립니다.
Adding unnecessary 저에게: 저에게 회신해 주세요.
회신 부탁드립니다 already implies 'to me'. The explicit 저에게 is heavy and redundant in business mail; drop it.
Mixing up 회신 and 답변.
회신 = a reply/getting back to you; 답변 = an answer to a specific question. If you asked something concrete, 답변 부탁드립니다; for general 'reply', 회신 부탁드립니다.

usage: Polite-formal; asks for a careful look + opinion
I'd appreciate it if you'd review it
Could you give it a look?
Lighter spoken-ish variant to a peer
Please review and share your feedback
Explicitly asks for comments after review
examples: 기획안 검토 부탁드립니다.
Please review the proposal.
Sends a document for the reader to examine critically
초안이라 부족한 부분이 많은데 검토 부탁드립니다.
It's a draft with many rough spots, so please review it.
초안 ('draft') framing explicitly invites correction — humble and real
A: 1차 기획안 공유드립니다. 검토 후 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다. / B: 읽어 보고 오후에 피드백 드릴게요.
A: Sharing the first draft. If you review and give feedback, I'll incorporate it. / B: I'll read it and give you feedback this afternoon.
A/B exchange: sending a draft for review and the senior's reply committing a feedback time
nuance: 검토 부탁드립니다 is 검토 ('review/examination', Sino-Korean 檢討) + 부탁드립니다, asking the reader to read something critically and weigh in. Unlike the lighter 확인 ('just check/confirm'), 검토 implies real scrutiny — reading a proposal, catching problems, forming an opinion — so it is sent to someone whose judgment you want, often a senior, and implicitly invites feedback or approval. That is the key contrast English speakers blur: 확인 부탁드립니다 = 'please confirm/glance', 검토 부탁드립니다 = 'please examine and judge'. Asking a boss to merely 확인 a strategy doc undersells what you need; 검토 is right. The register is humble (부탁드리다), fully appropriate upward. The English-speaker pitfall is the loanword 리뷰 (리뷰 부탁드립니다) — acceptable in casual startup culture but reads as Konglish in formal mail; use 검토. Another trap: confusing 검토 with 검사 (檢査, an INSPECTION or test — medical or quality) — 검사 부탁드립니다 sounds like requesting a lab test. 검토 is a 하다-noun: 검토하다, so 검토해 주세요 or 검토 부탁드립니다, never 검토 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 검토 부탁드립니다 asks the reader to read something critically and weigh in. 검토 implies real scrutiny — reading a proposal, catching problems, forming an opinion — not a light glance. It is sent to someone whose judgment you want, often a senior, and implicitly invites feedback or approval.

Humble 부탁드리다 makes it appropriate upward to bosses and clients. For maximum courtesy, upgrade to 검토해 주시면 감사하겠습니다. To peers, 한번 검토해 봐 주세요 is lighter and more conversational. For a document with a revision cycle, add: 검토 후 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다.
chips: 한번 검토해 봐 주세요 — peer level

structuredNuance.t: 확인 부탁드립니다 (light check/confirm) vs. 검토 부탁드립니다 (critical review with judgment) vs. 검사 부탁드립니다 (inspection/testing — wrong for documents). Using 확인 where 검토 is needed signals you just want acknowledgment, not analysis.
검토 부탁드립니다 → 검토해 주시면 감사하겠습니다 (conditional, most polite) → 검토 후 의견 부탁드립니다 (explicitly asks for comments) → 검토 후 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다 (full revision cycle phrase).

Do not use 리뷰 부탁드립니다 — 리뷰 is casual Konglish; formal mail uses 검토. Do not confuse 검토 with 검사 (檢査, inspection/testing) — 검사 부탁드립니다 sounds like requesting a medical or quality test. Do not say 검토 주세요 — 검토 is a 하다-noun; the verb form is 검토해 주세요.

mistakes: Using 확인 when you need real review.
확인 is a light check/confirm. For a critical read with feedback or approval, ask 검토 부탁드립니다, not 확인 부탁드립니다.
Writing 리뷰 부탁드립니다.
리뷰 is casual Konglish. Formal Korean business mail uses 검토 부탁드립니다.
Confusing 검토 with 검사.
검토 = reviewing/examining (a document, plan); 검사 = inspection/testing (quality, medical). 검사 부탁드립니다 sounds like requesting a test, not a document review.

english: I'd be grateful if you could check and reply
usage: I'd appreciate it if you'd check and reply
I'd be grateful if you'd check and contact me
연락 ('get in touch') instead of 회신
Once you reply, I'll proceed right away
Ties the reply to your next action
examples: 견적서 확인 후 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다.
I'd appreciate it if you'd review the quote and get back to me.
Common closing on a proposal or quote email
내용 확인 후 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다. 미리 감사드립니다.
I'd be grateful for your check and reply. Thank you in advance.
Advance thanks 미리 감사드립니다 adds a final courtesy layer
A: 바쁘시겠지만 확인 후 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다. / B: 확인 후 내일 오전 중으로 회신드리겠습니다.
A: I know you're busy, but I'd be grateful for your check and reply. / B: I'll check and reply by tomorrow morning.
A/B: the full polite-closer pattern and a professional reply committing a timeframe
nuance: 확인 후 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다 stacks 확인 ('check') + 후 ('after') + 회신 ('reply') + 주시면 ('if you would give/do') + 감사하겠습니다 ('I would be grateful'). The -(으)면 감사하겠습니다 frame is the gold-standard polite request in Korean business writing: it phrases your need as a conditional favor and thanks them in advance. This is gentler than a direct 부탁드립니다 and fits situations where maximum deference helps — clients, senior executives, first-contact emails. The contrast: 회신 부탁드립니다 is direct-polite ('please reply'), while 주시면 감사하겠습니다 is indirect-polite ('I'd be thankful if…') — the latter is a notch more formal and deferential. The English-speaker pitfall is mistranslating 'I would be grateful' as 저는 감사할 것입니다 (a flat future 'I will thank') — Korean uses the -겠- conjecture/intention form 감사하겠습니다, paired with the conditional 주시면. Dropping 주시면 (회신 감사하겠습니다) breaks the logic: it reads 'I'll be thankful for the reply' prematurely, as if they have already replied. Keep the 주시면 … 감사하겠습니다 pair intact.

structuredNuance.t: 확인 후 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다 is a polished, deferential closer meaning 'I'd appreciate it if you'd check and reply.' The -(으)면 감사하겠습니다 frame phrases your need as a conditional favor and thanks them in advance — the gold standard for maximum courtesy in Korean business writing.

Use this with clients, senior executives, or in first-contact emails where maximum deference is warranted. For standard internal mail, 확인 후 회신 부탁드립니다 is slightly more direct and equally acceptable. Combine with 바쁘시겠지만 at the start to cushion a deadline or urgency.
회신 부탁드립니다 (direct-polite) vs. 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다 (indirect-polite, conditional) vs. 회신 주시기 바랍니다 (formal/official written tone). The 주시면 감사하겠습니다 structure is the warmest and most deferential of the three.
확인 후 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다 → 검토 후 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다 (with heavier review) → 확인하시고 연락 주시면 감사하겠습니다 (연락 variant) → 회신 주시면 바로 진행하겠습니다 (ties reply to action). Append 미리 감사드립니다 for a final thanks.

Do not write 저는 감사할 것입니다 — use the -겠- form: 감사하겠습니다. Do not drop 주시면: 회신 감사하겠습니다 loses the conditional and sounds like premature thanks. Do not add 빨리 to soften urgency — 빨리 is pushy; use 가능한 한 빨리 or 바쁘시겠지만 + a deadline.

mistakes: Saying 저는 감사할 것입니다 for 'I would be grateful'.
Korean uses 감사하겠습니다 (the -겠- form) for 'I would be grateful', tied to a conditional 주시면. The literal future 감사할 것입니다 sounds wrong here.
Dropping 주시면: 확인 후 회신 감사하겠습니다.
Without the conditional 주시면 ('if you would'), the sentence loses its logic. Keep the pair: 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다.
Stacking it with a blunt 빨리: 빨리 회신 주시면 감사하겠습니다.
빨리 ('quickly') sounds pushy in a humble closer. If you need speed, use 가능한 한 빨리 or 바쁘시겠지만, not bare 빨리.

english: I think we'll need to coordinate the schedule
usage: I think we need to coordinate schedules
Polite-formal; raises a scheduling issue gently
More direct request to align timing
일정을 한번 맞춰 봐야 할 것 같아요
We should try to align our schedules
가능한 시간 알려 주시면 일정 조율하겠습니다
If you share your availability, I'll coordinate
Offers to do the coordinating yourself
examples: 담당자분들 시간이 달라서 일정 조율이 필요할 것 같습니다. 가능한 시간 알려 주세요.
Everyone's times differ, so I think we'll need to coordinate. Please share your availability.
Explains the reason then asks for free slots
회의 일정 관련해서 조율이 필요할 것 같습니다. 아래 시간 중 가능한 것 선택 부탁드립니다.
I think we'll need to coordinate regarding the meeting time. Please choose a slot from the options below.
Raises the need then immediately offers options — efficient business email pattern
A: 일정 조율이 필요할 것 같습니다. 다음 주 언제가 편하세요? / B: 화요일 오후나 목요일 오전이 괜찮습니다.
A: I think we'll need to coordinate schedules. When is convenient next week? / B: Tuesday afternoon or Thursday morning works for me.
A/B exchange: scheduling negotiation — the most natural use case for 조율
nuance: 일정 조율이 필요할 것 같습니다 is 일정 ('schedule', Sino-Korean 日程) + 조율 ('tuning/coordination', Sino-Korean 調律, originally 'tuning an instrument') + 이 필요하다 ('is needed') + -ㄹ 것 같다 ('seems/I think'). 조율 is the precise business word for negotiating and aligning times or terms among multiple parties — richer than just 'scheduling'. The -ㄹ 것 같습니다 ('it seems / I think') is doing important politeness work: Korean business culture prefers hedged, indirect phrasing. A flat 필요합니다 sounds blunt and presumptuous; 필요할 것 같습니다 ('I think it will be needed') is softer and collaborative. The contrast: 조율 (coordinating among parties, give-and-take) vs. 조정 (調整, adjusting or modifying a plan more unilaterally by one party) — for 'let's find a time that works for everyone', 조율 is natural. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'coordinate' as 협력하다 ('to cooperate', general teamwork) — that misses the time-alignment meaning entirely. Another trap: the particle — 일정 조율'이' 필요하다 (subject marker 이/가 on what is needed), not 일정 조율을 필요하다. The loanword 스케줄 is fine casually but 일정 is the professional term.

structuredNuance.t: 일정 조율이 필요할 것 같습니다 means 'I think we'll need to coordinate the schedule'. 조율 (調律) is the precise business word for negotiating and aligning times among multiple parties, not just setting one person's calendar. The -ㄹ 것 같습니다 hedge is essential politeness, softening 'we will need to' into 'I think we might need to'.

Polite-formal; safe upward and outward. The -ㄹ 것 같습니다 hedge fits all business contexts. To peers in a direct message, 일정 맞춰 봐야 할 것 같아요 is a softer spoken-style variant. The bare imperative 일정 조율해 주세요 ('please coordinate') is fine only downward.
chips: 일정 조율이 필요할 것 같습니다 — formal email
일정 맞춰 봐야 할 것 같아요 — casual/spoken
가능한 시간 알려 주시면 조율하겠습니다 — offer to coordinate yourself

structuredNuance.t: 조율 (調律, negotiating/aligning among multiple parties, give-and-take) vs. 조정 (調整, adjusting a plan more unilaterally) vs. 일정을 맞추다 (casual 'to align/match schedules'). For multi-party scheduling negotiation, 조율 is the professional choice.
일정 조율이 필요할 것 같습니다 → 일정 조율 부탁드립니다 (direct request) → 가능한 시간 알려 주시면 일정 조율하겠습니다 (offer to handle it) → 일정 조율 후 다시 안내드리겠습니다 (promise to follow up after coordinating internally).

Do not translate 'coordinate' as 협력하다 (that is general teamwork cooperation). Do not write the flat 일정 조율이 필요합니다 to a client — the hedge 것 같습니다 is expected. Do not use the loanword 스케줄 in formal mail — use 일정. Watch the particle: 일정 조율'이' 필요하다 (subject marker 이/가), not 조율'을' 필요하다.

mistakes: Writing flat 일정 조율이 필요합니다 to a client.
The bare assertion can feel blunt. Korean business prefers the hedged 필요할 것 같습니다 ('I think we'll need to'), which sounds more collaborative.
Using 협력 for 'coordinate the schedule'.
협력 ('cooperation') is about working together generally, not aligning times. For matching schedules, the word is 조율 (or 맞추다): 일정 조율.
Wrong particle: 일정 조율을 필요합니다.
필요하다 takes the subject marker 이/가 on what is needed: 일정 조율이 필요합니다, not 일정 조율을 필요합니다.

english: When would be a good time for you?
usage: Polite; asks the other person's availability
May I ask what time would work for you?
Proposing a specific day to narrow it down
examples: 미팅 잡으려고 하는데 언제 시간 괜찮으세요?
I'd like to set up a meeting — when are you free?
States the purpose first, then asks availability — the natural business order
혹시 다음 주에 언제 시간 괜찮으세요? 오전, 오후 중 편하신 때 알려 주세요.
Are you free sometime next week? Please let me know whether morning or afternoon works.
혹시 softens the question; offering two time windows narrows the back-and-forth
A: 언제 시간 괜찮으세요? 이 건으로 잠깐 통화드리고 싶어서요. / B: 내일 오후 두 시 이후면 괜찮습니다.
A: When are you free? I'd like a quick call about this matter. / B: After 2 p.m. tomorrow works for me.
Real A/B exchange: stating the reason for the call, then the other person proposing a specific slot
nuance: 언제 시간 괜찮으세요? is 언제 ('when') + 시간 ('time') + 괜찮으세요 (honorific '괜찮다', 'is it okay for you?'). It is the polite, natural way to ask someone's availability when arranging a meeting — literally 'when is your time okay?'. The honorific -으세요 on 괜찮다 directs the respect to the listener, so this is safe upward and to clients. A close variant is 언제가 편하세요? ('when is convenient?'), using 편하다 — slightly warmer and more considerate, stressing their comfort rather than just their schedule. The contrast: asking about THEIR availability (괜찮으세요 / 편하세요, honorific) vs. stating YOUR own availability (저는 ~ 괜찮아요 / 가능합니다) — keep the honorific form only for the other person. The English-speaker pitfall is the word 자유롭다 for 'free': 언제 자유로워요? means 'when are you free (as in liberated)?', not available — the correct words are 시간 괜찮다 / 시간 되다 / 한가하다. Another trap is dropping the honorific to a senior: 언제 시간 괜찮아? is 반말 and inappropriate in any work context.

structuredNuance.t: 언제 시간 괜찮으세요? literally means 'when is your time okay?' — the natural polite way to ask someone's availability for a meeting. The honorific -으세요 on 괜찮다 shows respect to the listener and makes the question safe for bosses, clients, and any senior person.

Safe upward and outward with the honorific -으세요. For maximum formality with executives, upgrade to 혹시 가능하신 시간이 언제일까요? The variant 언제가 편하세요? is slightly warmer, stressing their comfort. Never use 반말 괜찮아? in a work context, even with a close colleague in writing.

언제 시간 괜찮으세요? (open question, any time) vs. ○요일 어떠세요? (proposing a specific day) vs. 시간 되세요? ('does the time work?', equally common). The proposing form ○요일 어떠세요? is more efficient once you already know rough availability.
언제 시간 괜찮으세요? → 언제가 편하세요? → 혹시 가능하신 시간이 언제일까요? → ○요일 어떠세요? (propose a day). To narrow further: 오전/오후 중에 언제가 편하세요? ('morning or afternoon?'). Your own time: 저는 월요일 오후 이후 언제든 가능합니다.

Do not use 언제 자유로워요? — 자유롭다 means 'free as in liberty/freedom', not available. Use 시간 괜찮다 / 시간 되다 / 한가하다 for availability. Do not drop the honorific to a senior: 언제 괜찮아? is 반말. Do not apply the honorific -으세요 to your own time: only the other person's time gets the honorific.

mistakes: Saying 언제 자유로워요? for 'when are you free?'.
자유롭다 is 'free' as in liberty/freedom, not availability. Use 언제 시간 괜찮으세요? or 언제 시간 되세요?
Putting honorific on your own availability.
Honor the other person: 언제 괜찮으세요? For your own time, plain 저는 ~ 괜찮아요/가능합니다. Don't say 저는 괜찮으세요.
Dropping honorific to a senior: 언제 시간 괜찮아?
괜찮아 is 반말. To a boss or client use 괜찮으세요? or 편하세요?, never the casual 괜찮아.

english: I'd like to set up a meeting
usage: I'd like to schedule a meeting
미팅 한번 잡으면 좋을 것 같습니다
It'd be good to set up a meeting
Softer, suggestion-framed with 것 같다 hedge
May I set up a meeting?
I'll set the schedule and share it
When YOU will arrange and circulate it
examples: 이 건으로 회의 일정을 잡고 싶습니다. 언제 시간 괜찮으세요?
I'd like to set up a meeting about this matter. When are you free?
States the topic + immediately asks for availability — the most natural opening
관련해서 한번 모여서 논의하면 좋을 것 같아 회의 일정을 잡고 싶습니다.
I think it'd help to gather and discuss, so I'd like to schedule a meeting.
Gives the reason before proposing — softer and more justified
A: 가능하신 시간 몇 개 주시면 그에 맞춰 회의 일정을 잡겠습니다. / B: 화요일 오전이나 목요일 오후 괜찮습니다.
A: If you give me a few possible times, I'll set the meeting to match. / B: Tuesday morning or Thursday afternoon works.
A/B: invites slots and promises to finalize — the polite way to hand scheduling to the other party
nuance: 회의 일정을 잡고 싶습니다 is 회의 ('meeting', Sino-Korean 會議) + 일정 ('schedule') + 을 잡다 ('to set/fix') + -고 싶습니다 ('I would like to'). The verb 잡다 ('to catch/grab') is the idiomatic word for fixing or setting an appointment in Korean — 일정을 잡다, 약속을 잡다, 미팅을 잡다 — and English speakers rarely guess it. The -고 싶습니다 ('I'd like to') keeps it as a polite proposal rather than a command. The contrast: 회의 (a formal meeting, often internal, decision-making) vs. 미팅 (the loanword, often an external or more relaxed business meet-up) — both are common, but 회의 sounds more official/internal and 미팅 more flexible. The English-speaker pitfall is translating 'set up' as 설치하다 ('to install') or 준비하다 ('to prepare') — 회의를 설치하다 is wrong (that is for installing equipment), and while 회의를 준비하다 ('prepare a meeting') is possible, the standard scheduling verb is 잡다. Watch the particle — 일정'을' 잡다 (object 을/를), not 일정에 잡다. Also -고 싶습니다 marks YOUR desire; to ask if they would like to meet, say 회의 잡으실까요? or 시간 되실까요?.

structuredNuance.t: 회의 일정을 잡고 싶습니다 means 'I'd like to schedule a meeting'. The key idiom is 잡다 ('to catch/grab') as the standard verb for fixing an appointment — 일정을 잡다, 약속을 잡다. The -고 싶습니다 frames it as a polite desire/proposal rather than a command.

Polite-formal (합쇼체), safe upward and to clients. For extra deference, use the softer suggestion frame 미팅 한번 잡으면 좋을 것 같습니다. To ask permission from a very senior person: 회의 일정 잡아도 될까요? Never use 반말 잡자 in any professional email context.

잡으면 좋을 것 같습니다 — softer suggestion
회의 일정 잡아도 될까요? — asks permission

structuredNuance.t: 회의 (formal/internal) vs. 미팅 (external/casual, loanword). The verb 잡다 ('to set') vs. 준비하다 ('to prepare') vs. 설치하다 ('to install', wrong for meetings). Also: 회의를 열다 ('to hold/open a meeting') describes the meeting itself, while 일정을 잡다 is the scheduling step.
회의 일정을 잡고 싶습니다 → 미팅 한번 잡으면 좋을 것 같습니다 (softer) → 회의 일정 잡아도 될까요? (permission) → 일정 잡아서 공유드리겠습니다 (when you handle it). Paired naturally with: 언제 시간 괜찮으세요? immediately after.

Do not say 회의를 설치하고 싶습니다 — 설치하다 is 'to install equipment'. The scheduling verb is 잡다. Watch the particle: 일정'을' 잡다 (object marker), not 일정'에' 잡다. Do not use -고 싶습니다 about the other person; for their desire use 회의 잡으실까요? or 시간 되실까요?.

설치하다 is 'to install (equipment/software)'. To schedule a meeting, the verb is 잡다: 회의 일정을 잡고 싶습니다.
Wrong particle: 일정에 잡고 싶습니다.
잡다 takes the object marker: 일정을 잡다. The particle is 을/를, not 에.
Attaching 싶다 to the other person.
-고 싶다 expresses YOUR desire. To ask if they'd like to meet, use 회의 잡으실까요? or 시간 되실까요?, not '~고 싶으세요' phrased about them awkwardly.

usage: I'm informing you the schedule has changed
Adds the 'I'm letting you know' framing
We've unavoidably had to change the schedule
Would it be possible to change the schedule?
Asking, not announcing — requests a change
examples: 내부 사정으로 회의 일정이 변경되었습니다. 변경된 시간 확인 부탁드립니다.
Due to internal circumstances, the meeting schedule has changed. Please check the updated time.
States reason, announces change, requests confirmation — the full professional pattern
부득이하게 발표 일정이 다음 주로 변경되었습니다. 양해 부탁드립니다.
The presentation has unavoidably been moved to next week. Thank you for your understanding.
부득이하게 softens the announcement; 양해 부탁드립니다 completes the apology frame
A: 죄송하지만 일정이 변경되었습니다. 금요일 오후 두 시로 옮겨도 될까요? / B: 네, 괜찮습니다. 확인했습니다.
A: I'm sorry, but the schedule has changed. Would it be okay to move it to Friday at 2 p.m.? / B: Yes, that's fine. Noted.

nuance: 일정이 변경되었습니다 is 일정 ('schedule') + 이 (subject marker) + 변경되다 ('to be changed', Sino-Korean 變更 + passive 되다) in formal past. The passive 변경되었습니다 ('has been changed') is deliberate: it states the change as a neutral fact without pointing a finger at who caused it, which Korean business culture favors for delivering inconvenient news. If you say 일정을 변경했습니다 (active, 'I changed the schedule'), you take direct ownership — sometimes appropriate but the passive is safer. The contrast: 변경 (變更, formally changing/altering a plan) vs. 바꾸다 (the plain native 'to change/swap', casual) — in business email you write 변경되었습니다, not the casual 바꿨어요. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle and voice: 일정'이' 변경되었습니다 needs the subject marker 이/가 with the passive; the object marker 을/를 goes with the active voice (일정'을' 변경했습니다). Mixing them — 일정을 변경되었습니다 — is a classic grammar error. Always pair a schedule change with 양해 부탁드립니다 ('please understand') for courtesy.

structuredNuance.t: 일정이 변경되었습니다 announces 'the schedule has been changed'. The passive 변경되었습니다 is deliberate — it states a fact without assigning blame, which Korean business culture favors for inconvenient news. The active 일정을 변경했습니다 ('I changed it') takes direct ownership and is used when full transparency is needed.

Formal passive (변경되었습니다) for client- or senior-facing announcements. For a warmer, more apologetic tone add 부득이하게 at the start. Always follow with 양해 부탁드립니다 when the change inconveniences others. Casual internal note to peers: 일정이 바뀌었어요 is acceptable.

변경되다 (formal passive, Sino-Korean) vs. 바뀌다 (native-Korean passive, slightly more colloquial) vs. 바꾸다 (active, casual 'to change'). For professional email: 변경. For casual internal messages: 바뀌다 is fine. 바꾸다 (active) is only appropriate when owning the decision directly.

Watch the particle + voice pair: passive 변경되다 takes subject marker 이/가 (일정'이' 변경되었습니다); active 변경하다 takes object marker 을/를 (일정'을' 변경했습니다). Mixing them (일정을 변경되었습니다) is a classic grammar error. Also do not write the casual 바꿨어요 in a client email.

mistakes: Mixing voice/particle: 일정을 변경되었습니다.
Passive 변경되다 takes the subject marker: 일정'이' 변경되었습니다. The object marker 을/를 goes with active 일정'을' 변경했습니다.
Using casual 일정 바꿨어요 in formal mail.
바꾸다 is the plain/casual 'to change'. Professional email uses 변경: 일정이 변경되었습니다.
Announcing a change you caused with passive but no apology.
If you changed it and it inconveniences others, soften with 부득이하게 변경하게 되었습니다 and add 양해 부탁드립니다, rather than a cold passive alone.

Present form, heading a report email/message
I'll report as soon as results are in
examples: 오늘까지 진행된 내용 보고드립니다. 검토 부탁드립니다.
I'm reporting what has progressed so far today. Please review.
Report heading + a review request — the standard upward reporting pattern
말씀하신 건 확인해서 내일 오전 중으로 보고드리겠습니다.
I'll check the matter you mentioned and report by tomorrow morning.
Acknowledges a superior's request and commits to a specific report time
A: 진행 상황 어떻게 됩니까? / B: 현재 50% 완료되었습니다. 마무리되는 대로 바로 보고드리겠습니다.
A: How is the progress? / B: It is currently 50% complete. I will report to you as soon as it is finished.

nuance: 보고드리겠습니다 is 보고 ('report', Sino-Korean 報告) + 드리다 (the HUMBLE form of 주다 'to give', used when the recipient is senior) + -겠습니다 ('I will'). The 드리다 is the heart of it: it lowers YOU relative to the person you are reporting to, so 보고드리다 inherently means reporting UPWARD to a boss, client, or senior — you would never use it to a junior. The contrast: 보고드리다 (humble, upward) vs. plain 보고하다 (neutral 'to report', describing the act or used horizontally) vs. 알리다 ('to inform/notify', more horizontal). The English-speaker pitfall is using 보고하다 flatly to a boss (보고합니다 / 보고할게요) — not wrong, but the humble 보고드립니다 / 보고드리겠습니다 is the expected register upward in hierarchical Korean offices, and missing 드리다 can feel under-polite. Another trap: 보고 is a 하다/드리다-noun, so you say 보고드리다 or 보고하다, written as one word — never 보고를 드리다 split apart. Also note that 보고 (報告, report) differs entirely from the connective 보고 in 보고 싶다 ('want to see') — same romanization, different origin.

structuredNuance.t: 보고드리겠습니다 means 'I will report (to you)'. The 드리다 is the core: it is the humble form of 주다, lowering yourself toward the senior recipient. This makes 보고드리다 an inherently upward-directed verb — you report to your boss, not to a subordinate.

보고드리겠습니다 (future) → 보고드립니다 (present heading) → 진행 상황 보고드리겠습니다 (with topic) → 결과 나오면 바로 보고드리겠습니다 (immediate follow-up promise) → 확인 후 보고드리겠습니다 (after checking). All use the same 드리다 humble core.

Do not use the plain 보고합니다 upward if 보고드립니다 is expected — it can feel slightly under-polite in hierarchical offices. Do not split 보고를 드리다 apart — 보고드리다 is written as one verb. Do not confuse 보고 (報告, report) with the connective 보고 from 보다 (as in 보고 싶다, 'want to see').

mistakes: Using plain 보고합니다 to a senior.
To a boss/client the humble form 보고드립니다 / 보고드리겠습니다 (with 드리다) is expected. Plain 보고합니다 can feel under-polite upward.
Saying 보고드리겠습니다 to a junior.
드리다 lowers you toward a SENIOR. To a subordinate you wouldn't humble yourself; use 보고하다 or, depending on direction, just 알려 줄게요.
Confusing 보고 (報告) with 보고 (보다).
報告 = a report; 보고 in 보고 싶다 is the connective of 보다 ('see'). 보고드리겠습니다 means 'I'll report', not 'I want to see'.

usage: I'll check and contact you again
I'll look into it and get back to you
알아보다 ('look into') for things you must research
I'll contact you as soon as it's confirmed
-는 대로 ('as soon as') for prompt follow-up
Signals you must check with your team first
examples: 지금 바로 답변드리기 어려워서, 확인 후 다시 연락드리겠습니다.
It's hard to answer right now, so I'll check and contact you again.
Polite way to defer an immediate answer without being evasive
재고 상황 확인 후 오늘 중으로 다시 연락드리겠습니다.
I'll check the stock and get back to you within today.
Adds a specific time commitment — makes the promise concrete and trustworthy
A: 이 건 언제쯤 처리될까요? / B: 담당자에게 확인 후 내일까지 다시 연락드리겠습니다.
A: When do you think this matter will be handled? / B: I'll check with the person in charge and get back to you by tomorrow.
A/B: client asking for a timeline; staff deflecting politely and committing to a follow-up date
nuance: 확인 후 다시 연락드리겠습니다 is 확인 ('check') + 후 ('after') + 다시 ('again') + 연락 ('contact', Sino-Korean 連絡) + 드리다 (humble 'give/do for a senior') + -겠습니다 ('I will'). It is the courteous, professional way to say 'let me look into this and get back to you' — invaluable when you cannot answer on the spot. The humble 연락드리다 (vs. plain 연락하다) lowers you toward the client or senior, which is the expected register outward and upward. The contrast: 연락드리다 ('I'll contact you', humble, you reaching out first) vs. 회신드리다 ('I'll reply', responding specifically to their message) — both work, but 연락 is broader ('get in touch') while 회신 is 'a reply to your email'. The English-speaker pitfall is the calque 'get back to you' rendered as 돌아오겠습니다 ('I will physically return') — that sounds like coming back to a location, not following up; the idiom is 다시 연락드리겠습니다. Another trap is dropping 드리다 to a client (다시 연락하겠습니다) — understandable but less polite; 연락드리겠습니다 is the safe default. A bare 다시 연락드리겠습니다 with no timeframe can feel vague — add 오늘 중으로 / 내일까지 / 확인되는 대로 to make the promise concrete.

structuredNuance.t: 확인 후 다시 연락드리겠습니다 means 'I'll check and get back to you' — the courteous way to defer an immediate answer. The humble 드리다 lowers you toward the client or senior, signaling this is a service-minded promise, not just a statement of intent.

The humble 연락드리다 is essential upward and outward. Downward or to peers, plain 연락하겠습니다 / 연락할게요 is fine. Always add a timeframe (오늘 중으로, 내일까지, 확인되는 대로) so the promise does not feel vague. If the delay might be longer, explain why briefly.
chips: 확인되는 대로 연락드리겠습니다 — 'as soon as confirmed'

structuredNuance.t: 연락드리다 ('I'll contact you', humble, you initiate) vs. 회신드리다 ('I'll reply', responding to their message) vs. 알아보고 드리겠습니다 ('I'll look into it and let you know', 알아보다 stresses research). Use 알아보다 when you need to gather information before reporting back.
확인 후 다시 연락드리겠습니다 → 알아보고 연락드리겠습니다 (looking into something) → 확인되는 대로 연락드리겠습니다 (as soon as confirmed) → 내부적으로 확인 후 회신드리겠습니다 (internal check + formal reply). Add 오늘 중으로 / 내일까지 for a concrete commitment.

Do not say 다시 돌아오겠습니다 — 돌아오다 is 'to physically return'. The follow-up idiom is 다시 연락드리겠습니다. Do not drop 드리다 to a client — 연락드리겠습니다 not 연락하겠습니다. Do not leave the promise without a timeframe — 다시 연락드리겠습니다 alone sounds vague; add 오늘 중으로 or 확인되는 대로.

mistakes: Saying 다시 돌아오겠습니다 for 'I'll get back to you'.
돌아오다 is 'to physically return/come back'. To follow up, say 다시 연락드리겠습니다, not 돌아오겠습니다.
Dropping 드리다 to a client: 다시 연락하겠습니다.
To a client/senior the humble 연락드리겠습니다 is expected. Plain 연락하겠습니다 is fine internally but less courteous outward.
Promising follow-up with no timeframe.
다시 연락드리겠습니다 alone can feel vague. Add a window — 확인되는 대로 / 오늘 중으로 다시 연락드리겠습니다 — so the reader knows when to expect you.

english: May I ask how the matter I requested is going?
usage: How is the matter I asked about going?
Polite follow-up/nudge on a pending item
May I ask about the progress?
Would a reply on my previous email be possible?
I know you're busy, but I'm asking once more
Softener-led nudge for a slow reply
examples: 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만, 확인 부탁드린 건 어떻게 되었을까요?
Sorry to bother you when you're busy, but how is the matter I asked about going?
Face-saving softener before the nudge — essential when following up with a senior
저번에 보내드린 견적 관련해서 확인 부탁드린 건 어떻게 되었을까요? 일정이 있어 여쭤봅니다.
Regarding the quote I sent before, how is the matter going? I'm asking because there's a deadline.
Ties the nudge to a specific earlier document and gives a reason (deadline) — more persuasive than a bare follow-up
A: 지난주에 검토 부탁드린 기획안 어떻게 되었을까요? / B: 아, 죄송합니다. 내일 오전까지 피드백 드리겠습니다.
A: How is the proposal I asked you to review last week going? / B: Oh, I'm sorry. I'll give you feedback by tomorrow morning.
Real A/B exchange: gentle nudge and the recipient's apology + commitment — shows the softened form working as intended
nuance: 확인 부탁드린 건 어떻게 되었을까요? is 확인 부탁드린 ('that I asked you to check', relative clause) + 건 (contraction of 것은, 'the matter') + 어떻게 ('how') + 되었을까요 ('I wonder how it has come along', the speculative -을까요 form). ('why haven't you checked yet?') is accusatory; 어떻게 되었을까요? frames the same query as innocent curiosity. Also 됐어요? (flat 'is it done?') is too direct upward. The English-speaker pitfall is the impatient calque 'any update?' as bare 업데이트 있어요? — Konglish and curt; Korean wraps the nudge in indirectness. Always lead with a face-saving softener (바쁘시겠지만, 죄송하지만) before the question when nudging a senior.

structuredNuance.t: 확인 부탁드린 건 어떻게 되었을까요? is the diplomatic way to follow up on a pending request without sounding pushy. The speculative -을까요 ('I wonder if…') and the indirect 어떻게 되었- ('how has it come along') preserve the reader's face — a core value in Korean hierarchical culture.

Used upward or to clients when nudging a delayed response. Always lead with a softener: 바쁘시겠지만 / 죄송하지만. For an even gentler approach, use 혹시 진행 상황 여쭤봐도 될까요? (the humble ask-permission form). Never use bare 됐어요? or 왜 안 하셨어요? upward.
chips: 혹시 여쭤봐도 될까요? — asking permission to ask

structuredNuance.t: 어떻게 되었을까요? (speculative, gentle, face-preserving) vs. 됐어요? (flat 'done?', too direct upward) vs. 왜 아직 안 하셨어요? (accusatory, never use upward). In written email, 혹시 진행 상황 여쭤봐도 될까요? with humble 여쭤보다 is also excellent.
확인 부탁드린 건 어떻게 되었을까요? → 혹시 진행 상황 여쭤봐도 될까요? → 지난번 메일 관련 회신 가능하실까요? → 바쁘시겠지만 다시 한번 여쭤봅니다. All carry the same indirect-nudge function with varying levels of formality.

Do not write bare 업데이트 있어요? — Konglish and curt. Korean wraps the nudge in indirectness. Do not skip the softener (바쁘시겠지만 / 죄송하지만) before following up with a senior. Do not use 됐어요? or 왜 아직 확인 안 하셨어요? — these are too direct and can damage the relationship.

mistakes: Chasing with 왜 아직 확인 안 하셨어요?
That accuses the reader of failing to act. Use the face-saving 확인 부탁드린 건 어떻게 되었을까요? to nudge gently.
Writing bare 업데이트 있어요? for 'any update?'.
Konglish and curt. Korean phrases a status nudge indirectly: 진행 상황 여쭤봐도 될까요? or 어떻게 되었을까요?
Skipping a softener before nudging a senior.
Going straight to the question can sound impatient. Lead with 바쁘시겠지만 or 죄송하지만 to cushion the follow-up.

english: If you review and share feedback, I'll incorporate it
usage: I'll incorporate your feedback after you review
Polite; invites comments and promises to apply them
I'll revise if you give comments
I'll apply the feedback and re-share
When you'll send an updated version back
수정할 부분 알려 주시면 바로 반영하겠습니다
Tell me what to fix and I'll apply it right away
examples: 초안입니다. 검토 후 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다.
This is a draft. I'll incorporate your feedback after you review.
Classic draft-submission line — sends the document and opens the revision loop
부족한 부분 있으면 편하게 말씀해 주세요. 바로 반영하겠습니다.
If there are weak spots, feel free to let me know. I'll incorporate it right away.
Humble invitation: the 편하게 ('freely/comfortably') signals you welcome criticism
A: 1차 기획안 공유드립니다. 검토 후 의견 주시면 반영해서 2차 안 준비하겠습니다. / B: 읽어 보고 오늘 오후에 피드백 드릴게요.
A: Sharing the first draft. After review, I'll incorporate feedback into a second version. / B: I'll read it and give feedback this afternoon.
A/B: full revision cycle stated by the sender; senior commits a feedback time — the ideal exchange for a draft submission
nuance: 검토 후 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다 is 검토 ('review') + 후 ('after') + 의견 ('opinion/feedback', Sino-Korean 意見) + 주시면 ('if you would give') + 반영하겠습니다 ('I will reflect/incorporate', Sino-Korean 反映). The standout word is 반영하다 — literally 'to reflect (as in a mirror)', it is the precise business verb for incorporating feedback into a document, and English speakers almost never produce it naturally. The -주시면 … 반영하겠습니다 frame ('if you give … I'll incorporate') is collaborative and positions you as receptive. A named near-synonym expression is 코멘트 주시면 수정하겠습니다 ('if you give comments, I'll revise') — lighter and more casual (코멘트 is a loanword; 수정 focuses on the correction act itself), whereas 반영 captures the full loop of receiving input and weaving it in. The contrast: 반영하다 ('incorporate/apply feedback into the work') vs. 수정하다 (修正, 'to revise/correct' the document itself) vs. 적용하다 (適用, 'to apply' a rule or setting). For taking someone's comments and working them into a document, 반영 is the exact choice. The English-speaker pitfall is 포함하다 ('to include'): 의견을 포함하겠습니다 sounds like attaching their opinion verbatim rather than acting on it. Also: in business you ask for 의견 ('considered feedback'), not the casual 생각 ('thought'). 반영 is a 하다-noun; the collocation is 의견을 반영하다 (object 을/를).

structuredNuance.t: 검토 후 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다 means 'after you review, if you give feedback I'll incorporate it'. The key word is 반영하다 — literally 'to reflect (as in a mirror)', the precise business verb for working feedback into a document. It captures both receiving input and embedding it in the work.

Polite-formal (합쇼체), used when submitting a draft to a senior or client. The -주시면 … 반영하겠습니다 conditional is courteous and collaborative. For extra humility, add 부족한 부분이 많지만 ('though there are many shortcomings') before the line. To peers, the lighter 코멘트 주시면 수정할게요 is fine.
chips: 검토 후 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다 — formal draft submission
피드백 반영해서 다시 공유드리겠습니다 — after revision

structuredNuance.t: 반영하다 (incorporate feedback into the work) vs. 수정하다 (revise/correct the document itself) vs. 적용하다 (apply a rule/setting). The three often work together — you 반영 the 의견 by 수정하는 것 — but 반영 specifically frames the act of taking external input and weaving it in.
검토 후 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다 → 코멘트 주시면 수정하겠습니다 (loanword variant) → 피드백 반영해서 다시 공유드리겠습니다 (after revision, re-sharing) → 수정할 부분 알려 주시면 바로 반영하겠습니다 (asking for specific edit points).

Do not say 의견을 포함하겠습니다 — 포함하다 ('to include/contain') sounds like attaching their opinion as an appendix, not acting on it. The verb is 반영하다. Do not ask for 생각 instead of 의견 — 생각 is casual; business uses 의견. The particle is 의견'을' 반영하다 (object marker 을/를).

mistakes: Saying 의견을 포함하겠습니다 for 'incorporate feedback'.
포함하다 is 'to include/contain'. To actually work feedback into the document, the verb is 반영하다: 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다.
Asking for 생각 instead of 의견.
생각 ('thought') is casual. In business you request 의견 ('considered opinion/feedback'): 의견 주시면 반영하겠습니다.
Confusing 반영 with 수정.
반영하다 = incorporate (their feedback into the work); 수정하다 = revise/correct (the document). They pair — you 반영 the 의견 by 수정하는 것 — but use 반영 for 'apply the feedback'.

english: I'm sorry to bother you when you're so busy, but…
usage: Sorry to trouble you while you're busy, but
Polite softener before a request to a senior
I know you must be busy, but
I know it's a hassle, but
Apologizes for the inconvenience of the ask
Sorry to be a bother, but
examples: 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만, 잠깐 확인 부탁드려도 될까요?
Sorry to bother you while you're busy, but could I ask you to check quickly?
Softener + small request — the most common business usage
바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만, 이 건만 먼저 처리해 주실 수 있을까요?
Sorry to trouble you, but could you handle just this one thing first?
Softener before asking for priority — acknowledges you are asking for something extra
A: 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만, 내일 회의 자료 오늘까지 회신 가능하실까요? / B: 네, 오늘 오후까지 보내드리겠습니다.
A: I'm sorry to bother you when you're busy, but could you reply with tomorrow's materials by today? / B: Yes, I'll send it by this afternoon.
Real A/B: softener cushions a tight-deadline request; the senior's reply shows the formula worked — they committed rather than pushing back
nuance: 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만 is 바쁘신 (honorific 'busy') + 와중에 ('in the midst of', Sino-Korean 渦中 'whirlpool/turmoil') + 죄송하지만 ('I'm sorry, but'). It is a face-saving CUSHION placed before asking a senior or client for something — Korean business etiquette strongly favors acknowledging the other person's burden before adding to it. The honorific 바쁘'신' is essential: you honor THEIR busyness. The contrast: 와중에 specifically implies a hectic, turbulent stretch, slightly more vivid than the plain 바쁘시겠지만 ('you must be busy, but'); 와중에 is a touch more deferential. Do not confuse 와중 with 도중 (途中, 'on the way/midway in a process') — 와중 connotes commotion while 도중 is simply 'during/en route'. The English-speaker pitfall is omitting the cushion entirely and leading straight with the request — even if the request itself is polite, the lack of a softener sounds abrupt and demanding in Korean. Another pitfall is over-apologizing by stacking multiple softeners (죄송하지만 + 미안하지만 + 실례지만); pick one. Register note: 죄송하지만 (formal) outranks 미안하지만 (casual) upward — always use 죄송하지만 in business email.

structuredNuance.t: 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만 is a face-saving CUSHION placed before a request to a senior or client. It acknowledges their burden before adding to it — a non-negotiable step in Korean business etiquette. The honorific 바쁘'신' is essential: you honor their busyness, not your own.

Used in formal business email upward or to clients. 죄송하지만 (formal) is correct here; 미안하지만 (casual) is for friends. The shorter 바쁘시겠지만 is fine in email and even spoken requests. For extreme deference — a very senior executive — combine: 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만 번거로우시겠지만.
chips: 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만 — full, most deferential

structuredNuance.t: 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만 (cushion before a request to a senior, acknowledges their busy state) vs. 양해 부탁드립니다 (requests tolerance for an inconvenience you caused) vs. 번거로우시겠지만 (apologizes for the hassle of the ask itself). These serve related but different social functions — don't swap them.
바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만 → 바쁘시겠지만 (shorter) → 번거로우시겠지만 (apologizes for the bother) → 귀찮게 해 드려 죄송하지만 (personal apology variant). All work as pre-request cushions; use one at a time, never stack all at once.

Do not skip the cushion — even a polite request to a senior without a softener can read as demanding in Korean. Do not stack multiple apologies (죄송하지만 + 미안하지만 together); pick one. Do not use 미안하지만 in formal email — 죄송하지만 is the business-level form. Do not confuse 와중 (turmoil/commotion) with 도중 (en route/midway).

mistakes: Leading straight with the request, no cushion.
In Korean business, asking a senior bluntly feels demanding even if polite. Open with 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만 or 바쁘시겠지만 to soften.
Dropping the honorific: 바쁜 와중에.
You honor the reader's busyness: 바쁘'신' 와중에. Plain 바쁜 omits the respect due to a senior/client.
Confusing 와중 with 도중.
와중 (渦中) implies a hectic/turbulent stretch; 도중 (途中) just means 'midway/on the way'. For 'while you're busy', it's 바쁘신 와중에.

usage: Please understand / thank you for understanding
Polite-formal; asks forbearance for an inconvenience
Softer, slightly less stiff than 드립니다
I'd be grateful for your understanding
We ask for your kind understanding
examples: 답변이 늦어 죄송합니다. 양해 부탁드립니다.
Sorry for the late reply. Thank you for your understanding.
Pairs an apology with a request to understand — the standard two-step for any inconvenience
내부 사정으로 일정이 변경된 점 양해 부탁드리며, 추후 다시 안내드리겠습니다.
Please understand the schedule change due to internal circumstances; I'll inform you again later.
Business pattern: reason + 양해 부탁드리며 + promise to follow up
A: 처리가 이렇게 오래 걸리나요? / B: 죄송합니다, 내부 검토가 필요해서요. 양해 부탁드립니다. 내일 오전까지 처리하겠습니다.
A: Does it really take this long? / B: I'm sorry, internal review is required. Please bear with us. I'll handle it by tomorrow morning.
A/B: client expressing frustration; staff apologizing, explaining briefly, asking understanding, and committing to a deadline
nuance: 양해 부탁드립니다 is 양해 ('understanding/forbearance', Sino-Korean 諒解) + 부탁드립니다 ('I humbly ask'). It asks someone to TOLERATE an inconvenience you have caused — a delay, a change, a limitation. It is the courteous companion to an apology: 죄송합니다 (sorry) followed by 양해 부탁드립니다 (please bear with us). A named near-synonym expression is 양해해 주시면 감사하겠습니다 ('I'd be grateful if you'd understand') — the conditional -면 감사하겠습니다 frame is one notch more deferential than the direct 부탁드립니다, softening the ask into a wished-for favor rather than a request; use it when maximum courtesy is needed, such as in a client letter or formal announcement. The key contrast English speakers miss: 양해 vs. 이해 (理解). 이해 is 'comprehension' — grasping a concept or instructions; 양해 is 'forbearance/tolerance' for something that went sideways. Saying 이해 부탁드립니다 wrongly asks 'please comprehend this', when you actually mean 'please tolerate this hiccup'. Another contrast: 양해 부탁드립니다 (asking forbearance for an inconvenience you caused) vs. 바쁘신 와중에 죄송하지만 (a cushion before making a new request) — different social functions. The English-speaker pitfall is the literal 'thank you for your understanding' as 이해해 주셔서 감사합니다 — grammatical but subtly wrong because 이해 is about comprehension; the set business phrase is 양해 부탁드립니다. 양해 is a 하다-noun: verb is 양해하다, so 양해해 주세요 or 양해 부탁드립니다, never 양해 주세요.

structuredNuance.t: 양해 부탁드립니다 asks someone to TOLERATE an inconvenience you have caused. It is the courteous companion to an apology: 죄송합니다 + 양해 부탁드립니다 is the standard two-step for any delay, change, or limitation in Korean business communication.

Polite-formal (합쇼체), used upward and outward. Always pair with an explanation or apology — 양해 부탁드립니다 alone without context sounds like asking a favor out of nowhere. For announcements or notices, 널리 양해 부탁드립니다 adds the formal broadcast feel.

양해 (諒解, forbearance for an inconvenience) vs. 이해 (理解, comprehension of meaning/concept) vs. 용서 (容恕, forgiveness for a fault — stronger). Use 양해 when something is inconvenient; use 이해 when checking if instructions are clear; never use 용서 unless the mistake is serious.
양해 부탁드립니다 → 양해 부탁드려요 (softer) → 양해해 주시면 감사하겠습니다 (conditional, most courteous) → 널리 양해 부탁드립니다 (broadcast). Always precede with the reason: 일정이 늦어진 점 / 변경된 점 + 양해 부탁드립니다.

Do not use 이해 부탁드립니다 — 이해 is comprehension, not tolerance for an inconvenience. Do not say 이해해 주셔서 감사합니다 as 'thank you for your understanding' — it means 'thanks for comprehending', subtly off. Do not say 양해 주세요 — 양해 is a 하다-noun; use 양해해 주세요 or 양해 부탁드립니다.

mistakes: Saying 이해 부탁드립니다 to mean 'please understand (bear with us)'.
이해 is 'comprehension' (grasping meaning). For tolerating an inconvenience, use 양해: 양해 부탁드립니다.
Saying 양해 주세요.
양해 is a 하다-noun; you can't 'give' it. Use the verb: 양해해 주세요 or 양해 부탁드립니다.
Using 양해 with no apology or reason.
양해 asks forbearance for something. Pair it with a brief apology/reason — 늦어 죄송합니다, 양해 부탁드립니다 — or it sounds like asking a favor out of nowhere.

english: Please CC them (add to the CC line)
usage: Polite; asks to copy someone on the email
Please CC me from now on too
Asking to be kept in the loop going forward
examples: 박 과장님도 참조에 넣어 주세요. 이 건은 공유가 필요합니다.
Please CC Manager Park as well. This matter needs to be shared.
Asks to copy a specific person and gives a brief reason
이 건은 팀장님도 아셔야 해서 참조에 넣었습니다.
The team lead should know about this, so I CC'd them.
Explains WHY you copied someone — prevents the team lead from wondering why they received it
A: 다음 메일부터는 저도 참조에 넣어 주시겠어요? 진행 상황 파악이 필요해서요. / B: 네, 앞으로 참조에 넣겠습니다.
A: Could you CC me from the next email? I need to keep track of the progress. / B: Yes, I'll CC you going forward.
A/B: requesting to be added to the CC loop and the sender agreeing — the most practical daily use
nuance: 참조에 넣어 주세요 is 참조 ('CC/reference', Sino-Korean 參照) + 에 ('into') + 넣다 ('to put in') + 주세요 ('please'). In Korean email, 참조 (參照) is literally the CC field, and 참조에 넣다 ('put into CC') is the everyday office phrase for keeping someone in the loop. A named near-synonym expression is 참조 부탁드립니다 ('please CC [them]') — a more compact, formal variant that drops 넣어 and uses the humble 부탁드리다 frame instead; it is slightly more deferential and suits upward or client-facing requests, while 참조에 넣어 주세요 is the more explicit, instructional form. This is the critical contrast that trips English speakers: 참조 (參照, the CC line) vs. 참고 (參考, 'for your reference/FYI'). They look and sound nearly identical and both loosely translate as 'reference' in English, but 참조 = the CC recipients in an email header, while 참고 = 'please take note of this information'. Saying 참고에 넣어 주세요 is wrong — you do not 'put someone into FYI'. The other field terms to know: 받는 사람 (To), 참조 (CC), 숨은 참조 (BCC). The English-speaker pitfall is the loanword 씨씨에 넣어 주세요 — understood in casual chat but not standard business Korean; use 참조. The particle: 참조'에' 넣다 (location 'into the CC field'), not 참조를 넣다. To say you already copied someone: 참조에 넣었습니다 or 참조로 넣었습니다.

structuredNuance.t: 참조에 넣어 주세요 means 'please add [them] to the CC line'. 참조 (參照) is literally the CC field in Korean email, and 참조에 넣다 ('put into CC') is the standard business phrase. The other email field terms: 받는 사람 (To), 참조 (CC), 숨은 참조 (BCC).
참조에 넣어 주세요 is the everyday polite form. For a senior or client, upgrade to 참조에 넣어 주시겠어요? (more deferential). To state you CC'd someone: 참조에 넣었습니다. To request ongoing CC: 다음부터는 저도 참조 부탁드립니다.
chips: 참조로 넣었습니다 — stating you CC'd someone

structuredNuance.t: 참조 (參照, the CC line — a person is added to it) vs. 참고 (參考, FYI — information to note). These are the two most commonly confused terms in Korean email. A third: 숨은 참조 (BCC — blind carbon copy). Never use 참고에 넣어 주세요 — you do not 'put someone into FYI'.
참조에 넣어 주세요 → 참조에 넣어 주시겠어요? (more polite) → 참조로 넣었습니다 (stating you CC'd) → 다음부터는 저도 참조 부탁드립니다 (asking to be kept in loop) → 숨은 참조로 넣어 주세요 (BCC variant).

Do not confuse 참조 (CC line) with 참고 (FYI). 참고에 넣어 주세요 is wrong. Do not use the loanword 씨씨에 넣어 주세요 in formal email — use 참조. Watch the particle: 참조'에' 넣다 (location, into the field), not 참조를 넣다 when placing a person in the CC field.

mistakes: Confusing 참조 with 참고.
참조 (參照) is the CC line; 참고 (參考) is 'for your reference/FYI'. 참고에 넣어 주세요 is wrong — to CC someone, say 참조에 넣어 주세요.
Writing 씨씨에 넣어 주세요.
씨씨 (CC) is casual/Konglish. Standard business Korean uses 참조: 참조에 넣어 주세요.
Wrong particle: 참조를 넣어 주세요 (meaning to CC a person).
You put the person INTO the CC field: 참조'에' 넣어 주세요. The location particle 에 marks where they go.
